item.title: Contention-Aware Flexible Execution for Machine Learning Workloads
item.description: arXiv:2611.26840v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Concurrent kernel execution is a ubiquitous paradigm in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) across both training and inference. That said, concurrency causes potential slowdown as concurrent kernels contend for limited GPU resources (cores, caches, memory bandwidth), which are shared between these kernels rather than exclusively available to one, as in isolated execution. This raises an important research question: to what extent does concurrency slow down kernel execution and how can it be mitigated. To answer this question, our work presents two studies. First, we characterize concurrent kernel execution extensively for the first time, to our knowledge. We conduct not just performance analysis of concurrent kernels but also memory behavior under concurrency on state-of-the-art AMD Instinct MI300X GPUs designed for datacenter AI, using the AMD-internal millisecond sampler. Based on the observations, we share insights on the slowdown along two dimensions (memory vs. compute bound, large vs. small kernels) to inform future optimizations. Second, we put the derived insights to use, aiming to deliver higher performance via targeted, flexible overlap of ML operators. Frameworks today make the simple decision of early-first for concurrent kernels, which is suboptimal. Noticing the opportunity that ML dataflow has inherent flexibility in which operators can be overlapped and how hardware resources can be allocated, we deduce simple heuristics to tune both overlap anchors and resource allocation for concurrent kernels to improve performance. We evaluate our proposed contention-aware flexible execution (termed CAFEML) across a variety of ML scenarios (inference decode, inference prefill, training) and demonstrate a speedup of up to 13% end-to-end with simple scheduling changes and no kernel rewrites.
item.dc:creator: Marco Kurzynski, Shaizeen Aga, Di Wu

item.title: Joint SLA Admission and Risk Allocation for Cloud Resource Provisioning
item.description: arXiv:2611.26924v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cloud controllers must reserve enough CPU and memory to meet demand without leaving too much capacity idle. Under a shared service-level agreement (SLA), a shortage of CPU or memory (considered as resource) counts toward the same limit. Dividing the allowed shortage risk between them changes how much extra capacity each need. We study this choice when forecast-error histories are short or correlated over time. Our controller compares different approaches to split the allowed shortage risk between resources. For each split, the controller uses historical forecast errors to determine how much extra capacity to reserve. It checks whether the history is enough to support that split and its consistency across different parts of the history. Among the splits that pass, it chooses the one with the lowest combined cost of shortages and idle capacity. Otherwise, the controller continues serving the workload with a calibrated fallback. In our simulation, we set a joint SLA target of sufficient CPU and memory in at least 95% of time slots and used 192 hours of historical forecast errors to structure the controller. Compared with always using fallback, the controller reduced the time slots allocation with either of the resource shortage by 1.04 percentage points on average. This reduction came with a 0.0091 increase in normalized cost from shortages and idle capacity. In the Bitbrains trace, five nonoverlapping test windows did not provide clear evidence of whether shortages increased or decreased. We also examine how execution delays and adjustment limits affect this trade off.
item.dc:creator: Yihua Xu, Jize Li, Yan Lyu, Jiani He, You Lin, Shangjing Tang, Dishu Yang

item.title: Analysis of Multi-Client Inference Techniques for Vision-Language-Action Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.26944v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) are a new class of machine learning model for generalizable robot control. While they enable robots to perform complex tasks in unseen environments, serving VLAs leaves hardware idle between inference passes and under-utilized during inference. Serving multiple clients at once can improve utilization, but fundamental multi-client techniques such as batching and co-execution have not been characterized for VLAs. We therefore characterize the trade-offs these known techniques impose across latency, throughput, power, and hardware utilization. Our findings inform trade-offs and challenges for future multi-VLA serving systems.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: IEEE International Symposium on Workload Characterization (2026) pp. 675-678
item.dc:creator: Stefan de Lasa, Mohammadreza Mofayezi, Gennady Pekhimenko, Nandita Vijaykumar

item.title: Contexture: Runtime Context Eviction for High-Throughput Agent Serving
item.description: arXiv:2611.26980v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents such as Hermes, OpenClaw, and Codex repeatedly resend growing execution histories, increasing shared GPU key-value (KV) cache demand in high-bandwidth memory (HBM). We show that shared KV capacity limits agent-serving throughput. Existing context-reduction methods lack global cache-state visibility, while runtime KV managers lack tool-execution information. Tracing tokens to their originating tool operations reveals that later operations supersede earlier outputs and associated turns, identifying 64% of recorded final-history tokens as removal candidates. We present Contexture, a harness- and model-agnostic architecture for runtime context eviction. Contexture separates the harness's full conversation history from the model's execution context, reducing subsequent requests' KV demand without modifying harness logic or model execution. It combines tool-execution information with global visibility into shared KV pressure and prefix residency: supersession identifies removal candidates, while runtime state determines when removal justifies sacrificing cached computation. This coordination reduces memory demand and decode KV traffic while limiting re-prefill interference with concurrent decoding, without additional model calls or training. Across two models, two harnesses, and two benchmarks, Contexture improves throughput under SLO by 20-73% over the best of no eviction, harness compaction, AgentDiet, and Continuum, and by 7-63% over observation masking in five of eight configurations, and reduces GPU energy per completed session by up to 11%. It also raises throughput under SLO by 23% over LMCache alone on H100. Live-agent experiments show a mean accuracy improvement of 1.4 percentage points over unloaded no eviction, with a worst-case loss of 3.7 points, while observation masking loses 3-28 points.
item.dc:creator: Colin Hong, Bryan Shan, Wei Siong Pang, Chengzhi Lu, Xu Guo, Nitin Shivaraman, Tao Luo, Esha Choukse, Kisson Lin, Dmitrii Ustiugov

item.title: CTRL: Concurrent Training and Rollout for LLM Reinforcement Learning via GPU Co-Residency
item.description: arXiv:2611.27119v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training of large language models runs two GPU workloads with different hardware demands: rollout decoding, which is dominated by memory access and whose batch shrinks as responses finish, and a dense learner. Current systems either time-share every GPU between them, paying serial phases and switches, or split GPUs into pools whose sizes change only in whole devices. We present CTRL, which makes co-residency a third RL execution layout: every GPU runs a learner rank beside a persistent rollout engine, sharing the device under CUDA MPS. A host-owned learner makes the layout fit: optimizer state stays in host memory, and policy weights stream layer by layer through a bounded GPU window. A publication gate trains each ready batch first and waits only before releasing the next policy, keeping a dropless staleness bound. A step-time bound guides compute-share selection, and a GPU-time ledger explains overlap and sharing costs. On H100, A800, and RTX 4090 GPUs with Qwen3 models, CTRL achieves 1.11-2.24$\times$ the throughput of the stronger of verl's asynchronous baselines across 24 workload settings with the staleness limit set to two, and 1.23$\times$ verl's colocate_async on eight H100 GPUs. With the same learner, co-residency is 1.10-1.26$\times$ faster than time-sharing on all three platforms and 1.10-1.30$\times$ faster than the best measured whole-GPU split on H100 DAPO-Math workloads at 256-528 trajectories per step, on four and eight GPUs.
item.dc:creator: Ruijia Yang, Ruikai Li, Zeyi Wen

item.title: Improved (Minimum) Spanning Tree Construction in the HYBRID Model
item.description: arXiv:2611.27145v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the HYBRID$_0$ model, vertices exchange $O(\log n)$-bit messages in synchronous rounds, both along input edges (local communication) and directly to vertices whose IDs they know (global communication). The local capacity is the maximum number of messages a vertex may send per round to each input neighbor, and the global capacity is the maximum number of global messages it may send, and also receive, per round. The standard capacity is local capacity $O(1)$ and global capacity $O(\log n)$. A well-formed tree (WFT) is a virtual tree of maximum degree $O(1)$ and diameter $O(\log n)$. Known algorithms construct a spanning tree (ST) and a WFT either in $O(\log n)$ rounds with global capacity $O(\log^2 n)$ or with standard capacity in $O(\log^2 n)$ rounds. We give a randomized algorithm that constructs an ST and a WFT in every connected component of any graph in $O(\log n)$ rounds with high probability under standard capacity. Our approach is based on a $\Delta$-pseudo-spanning representation ($\Delta$-PSR): a virtual network of maximum degree $\Delta$ with restoration information, such that any spanning tree of this network can be restored to a spanning tree of the input graph in $O(\log n)$ rounds. The algorithm of G\"otte et al. can be viewed as constructing an $O(\log n)$-PSR, which accounts for its global capacity $O(\log^2 n)$. Our main contribution is to construct an $O(1)$-PSR in $O(\log n)$ rounds with standard capacity. As applications, for $k$ distinct edge weights and any integer $1\le p\le k$, we construct an exact minimum spanning tree in $O((k/p)\log n)$ rounds with local capacity $O(p)$ and global capacity $O(p\log n)$, and the same tradeoff applies to $(1+\epsilon)$-approximate minimum spanning trees. We also compute biconnected components, articulation points, and bridges in $O(\log n)$ rounds with standard capacity, down from the previous global capacity $O(\log^5 n)$.
item.dc:creator: Shoma Hiraoka, Naoki Kitamura, Taisuke Izumi

item.title: AceVLN: Asynchronous Cloud Edge Deployment of VLNs via Latent Scheduling and Compensation
item.description: arXiv:2611.27255v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cloud--edge deployment enables asynchronous dual-system VLN on resource-constrained robots, but inference and communication delays cause latent mismatch and navigation errors. Existing adaptation methods reuse historical guidance but cannot provide updated navigation information when it becomes inadequate. We propose AceVLN, a training-free framework for active latent refresh and edge-side compensation. Our analysis reveals that action-relevant mismatch is concentrated in a compact Critical Subspace and can be tracked through fast-system feature drift. Critical Feature Drift Entropy reflects navigation sensitivity and guides adaptive refresh, while Critical Drift Continuity indicates when recent latent updates can support compensation during latency spikes. AceVLN integrates subspace-decoupled mismatch modeling, entropy-guided refresh scheduling, and continuity-guided compensation. Experiments show that \textit{AceVLN} improves success rates by 1.7--2.4 percentage points over the strongest baselines, while reducing amortized computation time by 2.7--10.0\% and FLOPs by 18.4--22.3\%.
item.dc:creator: Zihao Zheng, Hangyu Cao, Yulong Han, Xichang Wu, Zhihao Mao, Maoliang Li, Jiayu Chen, Hailong Zou, Donggang Cao, Xuanzhe Liu, Hong Mei, Xiang Chen

item.title: Dugong: Composing Uncertified DAG Consensus
item.description: arXiv:2611.27473v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: There is a significant number of uncertified DAG consensus protocols spanning partial synchrony and asynchrony as well as crash, Byzantine, and hybrid fault models, yet each protocol is designed, proved, and implemented from scratch. We introduce Dugong, a single parameterized protocol that unifies uncertified DAG consensus protocols. Its core algorithm, the Decider can implement eight existing protocols and yields four new ones by just tuning its parameters. Given the property that DAGs decouple throughput from latency Dugong presents a simple trade-off between latency and resilience to network and node faults. An operator can adapt the parameters of their protocol epoch-by-epoch to adjust the resilience without needing to develop a new protocol or worry about throughput. Around the Decider, Dugong layers production feature mechanisms (adaptive leader scheduling, checkpoints, responsive liveness, and crash recovery) that provably compose with each other and with the Decider's configurations. We formalize Dugong in Lean 4, proving safety and liveness under the established definitions of Byzantine atomic broadcast, and identify and repair gaps in published proofs. Finally, we implement Dugong as a reusable Rust library paired with a discrete-event network simulator, enabling direct latency comparisons across network and fault models.
item.dc:creator: George Danezis, Lefteris Kokoris-Kogias, Alberto Sonnino

item.title: Isonomy: Isolating Every Request from Timing Side Channels at Nearly Full-Sharing Throughput in Multi-Instance LLM Prefill
item.description: arXiv:2611.27596v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many long prompts share a prefix, and reusing its cached keys and values saves prefill computation. A cache hit, however, makes the first token arrive earlier and can reveal that another request used the same prefix, so providers share the cache only within an account. Under least privilege, even permission to send and pay for requests should not expose other requests' prompts in the same account. This matters because agents send unreviewed requests carrying private data, resellers pool users behind one account, and creden-tials can be stolen. Isonomy therefore isolates each request by default and lets requests opt into explicit sharing groups. Rather than give up reuse, it keeps one cache shared across accounts and hides only hits on prefixes cached outside a request's group. We target deployments where clients cannot observe one another's load, because there it suffices to hide these hits in the request's own timing. On three commercial APIs, our listeners could not distinguish added prefill work from a short request beyond measurement noise. Built on vLLM, Isonomy's gateway applies the deployment's routing rule to load and visible cache entries only, which yields the instance where the request would run if hidden hits missed. On that instance, the prediction mode estimates when the first token would be ready from the queue and the visible prefix, and gates its release. The execution mode instead reserves the work a hidden hit skips and fills it with other requests' prompts where possible. In direct-probe tests on two, four, and eight instances with every request isolated, both modes kept the upper bound on a probe's advantage within measure-ment noise at both prefix lengths. At saturation, the prediction mode retains 0.98 of unprotected sharing's throughput on two workloads with account labels, whereas isolation by account retains 0.95, or 0.80 where more reuse crosses accounts.
item.dc:creator: Bowen Sun, Chaowei Xiao

item.title: IsoMoE: Placement-Invariant Hybrid CPU-GPU MoE Inference with Lossless 12-bit Experts
item.description: arXiv:2611.27604v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale model capacity at low computational cost. Hybrid CPU-GPU inference offloads some experts to the CPU, enabling a single GPU to run MoE models larger than its memory. Expert placement changes with free GPU memory and should only affect speed. However, the greedy decoding outputs of existing hybrid engines change with placement. This is because the two devices use different arithmetic to compute experts. In addition, decoding is limited by CPU memory bandwidth. Lossless compression reduces memory traffic, but the CPU decompresses entropy-coded formats too slowly to keep up with memory reads. To address these challenges, we propose IsoMoE, an efficient hybrid MoE inference system that guarantees that its outputs do not change with expert placement. IsoMoE introduces (i) a GPU expert kernel that bitwise replays the arithmetic of the CPU expert kernel, (ii) a memory layout that allows the CPU to efficiently compute lossless 12-bit experts using AVX-512 dot-product instructions, and (iii) a dual micro-batch pipeline that overlaps CPU and GPU computation without changing the outputs. Experimental results on three MoE models show that IsoMoE produces bitwise identical outputs across different expert placements. It is also faster than the fastest baseline in every setting, achieving an average decoding speedup of 1.26$\times$ and a maximum speedup of 1.54$\times$. Our source code is publicly available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/isomoe-artifact-9C21/.
item.dc:creator: Hang Gu, Teng Wang, Zhendong Zheng, Qianyu Cheng, Wenqi Lou, Lei Gong, Xi Li, Xuehai Zhou

item.title: Asynchronous Byzantine Lattice Agreement with Logarithmic Response Time and Optimal Resilience
item.description: arXiv:2611.27663v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Lattice agreement is a fundamental coordination primitive in which processes decide on comparable values rather than identical ones. In the asynchronous message-passing setting with Byzantine failures, existing algorithms either require authentication or do not simultaneously achieve optimal resilience and logarithmic response time. We present an asynchronous Byzantine lattice agreement algorithm that tolerates up to $f$ Byzantine failures among $n>3f$ processes, requires no authentication, and completes in $O(\log f)$ time. The algorithm builds on the classifier-tree framework of Attiya and Rachman, replacing shared-memory communication with quorum-based message passing. The main challenge is preserving the information-flow invariants underlying the classifier tree despite Byzantine behavior. To address this challenge, we introduce Supported Reliable Broadcast (SRB), a communication abstraction that combines reliable broadcast with protocol-specific admissibility checks. Messages are disseminated using reliable broadcast, but are delivered to the protocol only after verifying that they are consistent with previously propagated information about the sender's state. This prevents Byzantine processes from bypassing the information-flow guarantees required by the classifier tree. A central technical difficulty lies in breaking the apparent circular dependency between message delivery and admissibility: admissibility depends on local state established by previously delivered messages, while message delivery itself depends on admissibility. Our proof resolves this circularity by separating reliable dissemination from admissibility propagation, yielding a modular correctness argument.
item.dc:creator: Hagit Attiya, Yao David Kolegain, Arnaud Labourel, Alessia Milani

item.title: Weave: Routing-Adaptive Runtime Warp Scheduling for MoE Megakernels
item.description: arXiv:2611.27765v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture is widely used in mainstream large language models. Under expert parallelism (EP), state-of-the-art systems fuse each MoE layer into a persistent megakernel for high performance. By the nature of EP, each GPU's communication and computation volumes vary with the routing result. However, prior work either fixes how GPU resources are divided between communication and computation at compile time (e.g., MegaMoE), or adapts to runtime dynamism only at coarse-grained SM granularity (e.g., mKernel), dedicating whole SMs to communication and leaving their Tensor Cores idle. At the finer warp granularity within each SM, static warp schedules can neither match routing-dependent loads nor prevent warps from idling while waiting for inputs or after finishing their assigned work. Therefore, we propose Weave, an MoE megakernel with three key designs. First, a spatial schedule allocates resources between communication and computation at both SM and warp granularities to match each GPU's load. Second, a temporal schedule switches warp roles as execution progresses, enlisting all warps at the start and end of a layer and selectively handing output scatter to idle communication warps. Third, a fused cost model jointly selects both schedules per GPU at launch from runtime routing statistics. Across all evaluated platforms, Weave outperforms the strongest baselines: under EP8 over DeepGEMM-MegaMoE, it speeds up the MoE layer by 1.30x geomean and up to 1.97x on SM103, and by 1.24x geomean and up to 1.72x on SM90; under EP16 on CDNA3, it beats the fastest official RCCL+AITER baseline by 1.44x geomean (up to 2.87x; 1.67x over vLLM).
item.dc:creator: Ziyu Huang, Yangjie Zhou, Chenhao Zhu, Hongzhe Yan, Tianwei Qiao, Sicheng He, Zihan Liu, Peng Yu, Shulai Zhang, Xingxun Tang, Xinhao Luo, Minyi Guo, Xiu Lin, Yinghao Yu, Guodong Yang, Liping Zhang, Shixuan Sun, Qingyun Chen, Jingwen Leng

item.title: TriAxialKV: Toward Extreme Low-Precision KV-Cache Quantization for Agentic Inference Tasks
item.description: arXiv:2605.17170v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Agentic workloads have emerged as a major workload for LLM inference. They differ significantly from chat-only workloads, requiring long-context processing, the ability to handle multimodal inputs, and structured multi-turn interactions with tool calling capabilities. As a result, their context exhibits structure that can carry different importance along three key axes: temporal recency to the current turn, modality such as text or image tokens, and semantic role such as user queries, tool calls, observations, or reasoning. These axes capture distinct token behaviors and lead to different sensitivities to KV-cache compression. However, existing KV-cache quantization methods are typically homogeneous or exploit only heterogeneity on a single dimension, such as temporal proximity or modality, overlooking the interactions among them. To this end, we introduce TriAxialKV, a novel mixed-precision KV-cache quantization scheme that assigns each token a triaxial tag, calibrates per-tag sensitivity, and allocates INT2/INT4 bit-widths under a fixed memory budget. We implement TriAxialKV as an end-to-end serving system, comprising calibration, mixed-precision quantization and memory management, and custom fused Triton decode kernels. When using Qwen3-VL-32B-Thinking as a computer-use agent operating the OSWorld, TriAxialKV matches the accuracy of SGLang with BF16 KV cache while supporting 4.5$\times$ KV cache capacity and achieving 30% higher end-to-end throughput, when running on real GPU systems.
item.dc:creator: Hanzhang Shen, Haoran Wu, Yiren Zhao, Robert Mullins

item.title: One Behavior, Out of Order: Deterministic Execution and Parallel Simulation of ROS 2 Applications
item.description: arXiv:2611.26676v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: System-level simulation is widely used to validate robotic applications before hardware deployment. However, Robot Operating System 2 (ROS 2), a popular middleware for such applications, uses asynchronous publish-subscribe communication, which can make application behavior depend on scheduling and the platform. The behavior can then vary across runs and machines even with the same inputs. This nondeterminism makes faults hard to reproduce and tests unreliable. In this paper, we first give ROS 2 applications a lightweight coordination scheme in which every component, including event-driven ones, reads its inputs and writes its outputs at predefined time instants. By decoupling computation and communication, the scheme makes an application deterministic, that is, it always has one behavior for given inputs. Tests are thus repeatable, but for large applications they still take a long time. To speed up these tests, we then present an out-of-order parallel simulation algorithm. From the predefined read and write instants, it knows before the run which activations of components depend on which. It starts each activation as soon as those it depends on have finished. Finally, we implement the algorithm in a simulator that runs existing ROS 2 applications without any change to them or to ROS 2. We evaluate the simulator on industrial use cases and synthetic graphs. On the industrial use cases, it is up to 2.6 times faster than synchronous parallel simulation and needs an order of magnitude less memory for messages than asynchronous parallel simulation.
item.dc:creator: Chengzi Huang, Behnam Khodabandeloo, Duc Anh Nguyen, Chuanchao Gao, Wang Yi

item.title: PLoQ: A Prompt-Specific Low-Rank Basis for 4-bit Quantization of LLM Activations
item.description: arXiv:2611.27092v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Low-bit activation quantization of large language models remains challenging, as a small number of dominant directions dictate the quantization range. State-of-the-art methods isolate these directions in a high-precision subspace through transformations calibrated offline and folded into the weights, which fixes the subspace for all prompts, leaving each prompt's few unique directions unprotected, and rules it out wherever no weight can absorb the transformation. We present PLoQ, a prompt-adaptive low-rank decomposition that extracts the dominant activation components before quantization, quantizes them separately, and restores them within the layer's GEMM, without modifying the weights. The low-rank component's basis is estimated from each prompt during prefill and reused throughout decoding. At the same bit width as state-of-the-art mixed-precision quantization (4-bit weights, activations and K/V cache with an eighth of the channels at 8 bits, about 4.2 bits per activation on average), PLoQ outperforms it on all six Llama and Qwen models from 1B to 70B parameters, at up to 8k tokens (16k on two of them), recovering up to 46% of the perplexity that the state of the art still loses to 4-bit activations. On Llama-3.1-8B at 8k tokens it adds only 4% to prefill and 8% to decoding.
item.dc:creator: Faraz Tahmasebi, Michael Pellauer, Hyoukjun Kwon, Sitao Huang

item.title: Drive Failure and Lifetime Simulation in the Backblaze Drive Statistics Corpus, 2013-2026
item.description: arXiv:2611.27122v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Storage simulators estimate data-loss risk from assumptions about drive lifetimes and dependence between failures. We test these assumptions against Backblaze's daily records from April 2013 to June 2026: 504,624 data drives with usable power-on ages, 99 drive models, 2.0 million drive-years and 31,881 recorded failures, including removals of drives judged likely to fail. We test failure-count forecasts over nine successive years and forecast the drives already in service at each prediction date. Accounting for drive-model differences and attributes improves the score assigned to observed failure counts about 4.3 times as much as replacing a single Weibull with two competing Weibulls under the same drive-model treatment. Fleet failure risk falls early and rises at older ages, but the fixed bathtub benchmark predicts 2.4 times the observed failures. Across 169 well-observed drive-model years selected using earlier records, 95% prediction intervals cover 44% of observed counts without annual variation and 92% with fleet-wide changes and shared good or bad years for each drive model. For drives already in service, a SMART warning raises one-year failure-risk ranking AUC from 0.64 to 0.73. Boosted trees using monthly SMART records give the best individual probability forecasts, yet predict 19% too many failures at one year and 22% too many at 90 days. Long-term survival depends on how aging is separated from calendar time: fitted fifteen-year survival probabilities differ by up to 18 percentage points, and assumptions about future calendar trends by up to 27 points. We provide samplers for storage simulations that represent drive-model differences, shared risks, and changes in drive condition.
item.dc:creator: Ahmed Amer, Darrell D. E. Long

item.title: Learning in Symbiosis: Heterogeneous Federated Learning with ANNs and SNNs
item.description: arXiv:2611.27686v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs), widely regarded as the third generation of neural networks, represent a promising neuromorphic computing paradigm with the potential to reduce the energy footprint of Artificial Intelligence (AI). Their en-ergy efficiency makes SNNs particularly attractive for resource-constrained Edge AI devices, motivating growing research interest in Federated Learning (FL) with SNNs. Despite these advantages, integrating SNNs into existing FL systems remains challenging, as replacing all conventional Artificial Neural Network (ANN) devices with SNN-based alternatives is impractical. Instead, we envision a gradual transition toward neuromorphic Edge AI, where ANN and SNN devices coexist and collaboratively participate in FL. To facilitate this transition, we propose Hybrid Neuromorphic Federated Learning (HNFL), a framework that enables joint training of heterogeneous ANN and SNN devices within an FL environment. Through experiments on CIFAR-10 using both VGG9 and ResNet architectures, we demonstrate the mutual benefits of collaborative ANN-SNN training. Specifically, HNFL achieves an average improvement of 16.85% when incorporating SNN devices into ANN-based FL and 8.02% when incorporating ANN devices into SNN-based FL. Furthermore, HNFL produces sparser spiking activity in the trained SNN models, with reductions of 12.4% for SResNet and 22.4% for SVGG9. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to demonstrate that ANNs and SNNs can coexist and mutually benefit from collaborative training in FL, providing a practical path toward the gradual integration of neuromorphic computing into existing Edge AI systems.
item.dc:creator: Manh V. Nguyen, Liang Zhao, Bobin Deng, Xinyue Zhang, Shaoen Wu

item.title: Discrete Incremental Voting: New Bounds for General Graphs and Expanders
item.description: arXiv:2606.06381v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We analyze the discrete incremental voting process (DIV) introduced by Cooper, Radzik, and Shiraga [OPODIS '23]. In this process, we consider a set $V$ of $n$ nodes connected in an undirected graph $G = (V, E)$ where each node has an integer opinion. In one step a randomly selected node interacts with its randomly selected neighbor and changes its opinion by $1$ in the direction of the neighbour's opinion. The process converges to a unique opinion that, in expectation, is the degree-weighted average of the initial opinions. We show that if the graph has conductance $\Phi(G)$, the ratio of the average to smallest degree is $\gamma(G)$, and the maximal difference between initial opinions is $K$, then the expected convergence time is ${O}\left({n\left(K\log (Kn)+\gamma(G) n \right)}/{\Phi(G)^2}\right)$. This bound is essentially optimal for a large class of graphs of bounded expansion. We also show that for regular graphs, if the second largest eigenvalue is $o(1/\log^4 n)$ and $K$ is $o\left({n}/{\log^2 n}\right)$, then w.h.p.\ DIV converges to the initial average opinion (rounded up or down).
item.dc:creator: Petra Berenbrink, Colin Cooper, Thorsten G\"otte, Lukas Hintze, Tomasz Radzik

item.title: Flying over The Uncertain Nature (FORTUNE): Intelligent and Humanistic 3D Path Planning for Low-Altitude Collaboration
item.description: arXiv:2608.03408v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Low-altitude intelligent agents are driving demand for timely, socially responsible collaborative sensing in dynamic urban environments. Yet jointly handling heterogeneous spatio-temporal sensing demands, real-time uncertainty, and human-centered constraints in a unified multi-uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) framework remains challenging. We study 3D multi-UAV path planning and joint task assignment under heterogeneous spatio-temporal uncertainty of ground points of interest (PoIs). Unlike studies assuming static, known PoIs, we formulate a unified model capturing persistent (Type-I), temporally predictable (Type-II), and emergent unpredictable (Type-III) demands. Following the low-altitude-for-good principle, we explicitly model altitude-dependent societal and environmental costs, including noise and public safety risks, jointly optimizing sensing effectiveness and socially compliant operations. To solve the resulting large-scale mixed-integer nonlinear problem, we propose FORTUNE, a hierarchical offline-online framework. Offline, a Transformer-based predictor forecasts Type-II activation windows, while an enhanced sparrow search algorithm (ES2A) with priority-aware decoding and danger-aware evolution generates globally coordinated flight plans. Online, lightweight trajectory refinement accommodates new Type-III PoIs while preserving global mission coherence. Experiments on real-world traffic and synthetic datasets show FORTUNE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art benchmarks, validating effectiveness, scalability, and practical applicability in dynamic low-altitude systems.
item.dc:creator: Wenbo Zhu, Wenhan Jia, Minghui Liwang, Yiguang Hong

item.title: Adaptive Determinantal Client Scheduling in Federated Learning
item.description: arXiv:2609.23843v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Scheduling clients for model training is critical in federated learning due to both data and system heterogeneity. Most previous works focus on the quality of the scheduled clients to achieve faster convergence, shorter wall-clock convergence time, or better average model performance. They rarely consider the diversity of clients, which is important to counter heterogeneity and improve performance for the worst-off clients. In this work, we advocate the use of determinantal point processes (DPPs) to model and enhance the diversity in client scheduling. We first design the kernel matrices of DPPs using gradient information and quality scores, which inherently enables a flexible quality-diversity trade-off. Applying fast MAP inference over DPPs, we propose Adaptive Determinantal Client Scheduling (ADCS) in FL. We further quantify the gradient approximation error of ADCS and develop convergence analysis for general biased client selection in FL with non-convex loss functions. We conduct comparative numerical experiments showing that ADCS outperforms state-of-the-art client scheduling algorithms, including both quality-based and diversity-based ones.
item.dc:creator: Wen Xu, Ben Liang, Gary Boudreau, Hamza Sokun

item.title: Eliminating Servers in State Machine Replication
item.description: arXiv:2611.01363v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: State Machine Replication (SMR) underpins many stateful systems, including distributed databases, coordination services, and metadata stores. Fundamentally, SMR requires state to be materialized from a durable total order of commands. Existing SMR systems rely on servers to materialize, locally store, and serve snapshots of state; while the durable total order either resides on the same servers, or on an external, disaggregated shared log. Unfortunately, servers act as brittle, expensive choke-points in such systems, causing service unavailability when they fail; incurring provisioning latency on cold starts; and red-lining when exposed to bad clients. In this paper, we propose Serverless SMR (S^2MR), where both the materialized state and the durable total order are stored on disaggregated storage; clients concurrently maintain a single copy of materialized state on external storage. Our key technical insight is that the shared log abstraction is useful not just for consistently ordering commands in SMR, but also for enabling distributed materialization, thus becoming the only interface for ac hieving SMR. We demonstrate S^2MR by developing AirDB, a transactional key-value store. In our evaluation, AirD B over S^2MR achieves higher availability than existing SMR-based systems like etcd over Raft: it is oblivious to server failures and bad client activity; and spins up 10x-45x faster from a cold start.
item.dc:creator: Dohyun Park, Wenjie Hu, Mahesh Balakrishnan, Yongjoo Park

item.title: Omakase: Execution Congestion Control through Conflict-Graph Integration in Multi-Proposer Blockchain
item.description: arXiv:2611.17184v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: As multi-proposer protocols push consensus throughput, transaction execution has become the dominant bottleneck in blockchains. Layer-1 blockchains parallelize execution either pessimistically (Solana, Sui), requiring upfront state-access declarations and serializing contended transactions, or optimistically (Aptos, Sei, Monad), resolving dependencies at run time but suffering cascading aborts under contention. Both treat blocks in isolation, leaving inter-block parallelism unexploited and most cores idle. We introduce Omakase, a parallel execution framework that combines pre-execution, inter-block conflict-graph integration, and graph-aware Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC). Replicas use idle cores to pre-execute only the blocks they propose, spreading prediction work across concurrent proposers. After building per-block conflict graphs and identifying their hot resources, a greedy scheduler integrates graphs across the blocks committed in a round, keeping an integration only when a lightweight balance heuristic predicts a parallelism gain. A graph-aware OCC executor then runs the integrated graph, admitting transactions in dependency order, which eliminates aborts when the predicted graph is exact and reduces re-executions when it is not. On 15,000 Ethereum mainnet blocks (~2.4M transactions) and synthetic workloads with configurable contention, Omakase reaches a 2.47x speedup over sequential execution, well above single-block OCC and graph-aware baselines. Against the strongest alternative, which runs the whole round as one optimistic window, Omakase matches mean throughput but is markedly more stable under high contention, because integration bounds how much optimistic work is in flight: this is the congestion control of our title. Integration is not free, but overlapping it with execution across rounds hides 94% of its measured cost in the validator pipeline.
item.dc:creator: Dakai Kang, Ray Neiheiser, Alberto Sonnino, Eleftherios Kokoris Kogias, Mohammad Sadoghi

item.title: AscendGYM: A Cost-Aware Kernel Optimization Benchmark for Real-World Workloads on Ascend NPUs
item.description: arXiv:2611.17621v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Kernel optimization is essential for efficient large language model (LLM) training and inference on Ascend NPUs. Existing Ascend kernel benchmarks primarily focus on kernel generation, with less emphasis on the ability of agents to optimize existing implementations under input configurations drawn from real workloads. To address this requirement, we introduce AscendGYM, a benchmark whose initial suite comprises 48 kernels across three difficulty levels. Each kernel is paired with test cases whose data types and tensor shapes are collected from real-world training and inference tasks. Consequently, performance improvements on AscendGYM map directly to the corresponding workloads. In terms of usability, two evaluation modes are supported in AscendGYM: model evaluation and model-harness evaluation. The kernel optimization capabilities of both trained models and custom agents are allowed to be measured. It provides a complete execution environment that closely reproduces how Ascend kernels are invoked in practical pipelines. For model evaluation, it additionally includes a built-in harness equipped with search orchestration and experience accumulation. Finally, we propose a new metric, the Speedup-Token Score (STS), which quantifies performance gains relative to token cost. By jointly considering speedup and cost, STS enables the assessment of practical kernel optimization capability of a model or harness under an acceptable budget. AscendGYM is available at https://github.com/SLAI-AITP/AscendGYM.
